title: Separating configuration from code in caching model output by input hash
spec: Describe how caching model output by input hash should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. Near-identical inputs miss, so the hit rate is worse than it looks. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The caching model output by input hash must store its input-to-output mapping logic and sensitivity thresholds in an external configuration source like a mounted volume or environment variables to ensure behavior changes without a rebuild. One setting that must never be baked into the binary is the input normalization or pre-processing parameters, such as rounding precision or whitespace trimming rules, because changing these values alters the resulting input hash and causes near-identical inputs to miss the cache. If the normalization parameters are hardcoded, any attempt to tune the sensitivity of the hash to increase hit rates would require a full recompilation and redeployment of the service, defeating the purpose of externalized configuration. By keeping these parameters in an external source, an operator can adjust the granularity of the input hash to balance between cache hits and collision risks without a rebuild. When the system reads these settings at runtime, it can apply different normalization steps to the incoming data before generating the hash, allowing for fine-grained control over how much variance is tolerated in the input. If the settings were baked into the binary, a developer would have to commit code changes and trigger a CI/CD pipeline just to adjust a rounding decimal, which is inefficient for production tuning. Because near-identical inputs currently miss due to rigid hashing, externalizing the normalization logic allows for immediate adjustments to the input-to-hash pipeline to improve the hit rate. This separation ensures that the core caching engine remains stable while the business logic of what constitutes a unique input can be tuned dynamically.
